abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for analyzing the topological structure of high-dimensional polytopes through the lens of discrete differential geometry. Traditional approaches to polytope classification rely heavily on combinatorial properties or metric invariants, often overlooking the intricate interplay between discrete curvature and algebraic structure. We propose the concept of discrete Weingarten maps on polytopal surfaces, establishing a rigorous connection between discrete geometry and algebraic geometry that yields new classification criteria for polytope families. Our main result demonstrates that the sequence of discrete Gaussian curvatures across face types satisfies a polynomial invariant relation dependent solely on vertex valences. This discovery enables a fundamentally different perspective on the Euler-Poincaré correspondence, revealing that polytope topology can be characterized through local geometric operators rather than global combinatorial counts. We further prove that this invariant distinguishes non-combinatorially-equivalent polytopes that were previously indistinguishable using classical methods. The framework opens new avenues for computational geometry by providing explicit algorithms to compute these invariants in O(n^d/2) time for d-dimensional polytopes with n vertices, significantly faster than existing methods. This work represents a paradigm shift in how we understand the fundamental relationship between discrete curvature phenomena and algebraic invariants in geometric structures.

We present significant theoretical improvements to the analysis of Delaunay triangulation stability under geometric perturbations. While previous work established qualitative stability bounds for Delaunay triangulations in Euclidean spaces, the quantitative dependence on point set motion remained poorly understood, limiting practical applications in computational geometry. We develop a refined perturbation analysis framework using the concept of theta-smoothness of the Delaunay graph, demonstrating that the Fréchet distance between the Delaunay triangulation and its perturbed counterpart is bounded by O(ε · log(1/ε)) under ε-perturbations of the input points, improving upon the previous O(ε^1/d) bound for d-dimensional spaces. Our analysis introduces a new local refinement technique that tracks the evolution of Delaunay simplices through a continuous lifting map to the paraboloid, revealing that the stability bound is fundamentally tied to the local circumradius-to-edge ratio. We further extend these results to weighted Delaunay triangulations and demonstrate their applications in mesh generation and geometric optimization. The improved bounds have direct implications for the design of robust geometric algorithms, as they provide tighter certificates for triangulation correctness in floating-point implementations. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical predictions and show that the new bounds are tight up to constant factors.

We introduce a new computational paradigm for geometric optimization problems based on the principle of kinetic triangulation maintenance. Traditional approaches to dynamic geometric problems treat geometric events as discrete disruptions requiring complete reconstruction, leading to inefficient O(n log n) update times even for simple geometric transformations. Our system, called Kinetop, reimagines geometric computation by maintaining a continuous representation of geometric relationships through differential algebraic equations rather than discrete event simulation. The core innovation lies in our concept of persistent geometric invariants—continuous quantities that remain invariant under smooth deformations and can be monitored through polynomial-time numerical methods. We demonstrate this paradigm through three fundamental problems: convex hull maintenance under linear motion, nearest neighbor tracking in streaming settings, and facility location under continuous demand evolution. For convex hull maintenance, Kinetop achieves amortized O(log n) update time, compared to the Ω(n) worst-case of traditional methods, by tracking hull evolution through tangent space dynamics. The system includes a complete software library implementing our approach with a domain-specific language for specifying kinetic constraints. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets show that Kinetop achieves speedups of 10-100x over state-of-the-art libraries while maintaining provable correctness guarantees. This work establishes kinetic computation as a new fundamental approach to computational geometry.

This paper presents PolyMesh++, a substantially improved system for high-quality polygon mesh generation with guaranteed geometric and topological guarantees. Existing mesh generation algorithms face a fundamental tension between mesh quality and computational efficiency, particularly when handling complex CAD models with sharp features and mixed element type requirements. We introduce a hierarchical refinement strategy that adaptively identifies geometrically critical regions requiring high-resolution discretization while exploiting smoothness elsewhere. The key algorithmic contribution is a novel feature detection mechanism based on discrete normal bundle analysis, which identifies geometrically significant curves and vertices with O(n log n) preprocessing time. Our refinement engine combines constrained Delaunay triangulation with local mesh improvement operations, maintaining all geometric constraints while achieving element quality metrics exceeding conventional approaches. We prove that PolyMesh++ produces meshes with bounded element quality (minimum angle > 25°) and bounded element size gradation, providing theoretical guarantees previously achieved only by quadratic-time algorithms. The implementation includes parallel processing capabilities utilizing space-filling curve partitioning for load balancing. Extensive benchmarking on standard mesh generation test suites demonstrates that PolyMesh++ achieves a 35% reduction in element count for equivalent accuracy compared to Gmsh, while running 2.5x faster on multi-core architectures. The system is publicly available and has been adopted by several computational engineering workflows requiring certified mesh quality.
